en: Ekajaṭākalpa, MS Kaiser 742 = NGMPP C 73/6; input by Péter-Dániel Szántó.
Budapest, February 2014.
Silent corrections and emendations.
Paper; common Newari script; 14 folios, of which the first is missing.
The first two folios of this bundle contain a sketch of the *Yogāmbara* maṇḍala with the names of 104 deities.

[On the fifth, eighth, and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight], one should draw it using powder of five colors; then, in the center of the inner maṇḍala, one should depict the Blessed Buddha, seated upon a white lotus (*pauṇḍarīka*), teaching the Dharma.

On the right side, one should have the noble Avalokiteśvara depicted, white as an autumn reed, wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment and white robes, with a white sacred thread; he should grant the gesture of fearlessness with his right hand and hold a lotus in his left. On the second [lotus], slightly below, one should paint the noble lady Tārā, endowed with inconceivable qualities, granting fearlessness, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a white silk upper garment, and holding a blue lotus in her hand.

On his right side, seated upon a peacock, is [Cundā], somewhat deformed, fierce, with terrifying fangs, adorned with ornaments of snakes, wearing a tiger-skin garment and an elephant-hide upper cloth, with a serpent as her sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), causing fear to all beings, holding a skull-cup in her hand, her body covered by her tongue, her mouth dripping with blood, three-eyed, and four-armed. With her first hand she grants boons; in the second is an axe (*paraśu*); in the third, a trident (*triśūla*); and in the fourth hand, a noose (*pāśa*). Her gaze is fixed upon the practitioner (*sādhaka*). There are two excellent female gatekeepers, Jayā and Vijayā, and four maidservants (*ceṭikā*): one should depict the maidservants Bhadrā, Siddhā, Viśālā, and Virajā.
The lotus-like faces should be depicted with tongues curled back and blood dripping from them; [these] lotuses are to be placed below.
Should they be *padminīs*?

This entire passage must concern Ekajaṭā: one should draw Indra’s vajra at the eastern gate all around the central maṇḍala. In the southeast, one should draw either Agni or a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). In the south, a staff (daṇḍa). In the southwest, a mace (taṣṭra). In the west, a noose (pāśa). In the northwest, a banner (patāka) or [the symbol of] Jaina (?). In the north, a citron (bījapūraka). In the northeast, one should draw a trident (triśūla).

[Then, having drawn the complete maṇḍala and performed the royal worship according to the procedure prescribed in the tantra, one should take the *argha* offering, pay homage, and begin the invocation:

Oṃ, homage to Amitābha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! Tara 2, Vidhama 2, Satya 2, Tapa 2, Dhama 2, Jñāna 2! O you who look upon the light and the darkness, O bearer of Dharma, O bearer of knowledge, O you who cause the destruction of saṃsāra, O liberator of all sentient beings! Oṃ, come here, Blessed One; homage be to you, svāhā!
The invocation mantra of the Blessed Buddha. It should be performed together with the mudrā of the Blessed One:

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, to the Three Jewels, to the Bodhisattva, the Great Being, the Great Compassionate One! Oṃ, lotus, lotus! Great lotus! To him who holds the excellent tip of a lotus in his hand: move, move! Come, come! Fill this maṇḍala yourself! May there be accomplishment! Take away, take away! Move, move! Homage be to you, the one of ultimate compassion! Svāhā!
This is the invocation mantra of Noble Avalokiteśvara.
Oṃ tāre tāravare, come here, O Blessed One, svāhā!
This is the invocation mantra of the Blessed Noble Tārā.
First is the salutation:
*Nama ekajaṭāyai mahārākṣasyai ehy ehi bodhisattvājñākarīye svāhā*. *Anantāyai svāhā*. *Jayāyai svāhā*. *Vijayāyai svāhā*. *Jayavijayāyai sarvārthaṃ me sādhaya svāhā*.
This is the mantra for the invocation of Ekajaṭā:

Homage to the Triple Gem! To Ekajaṭā: Hrīḥ! Summon, summon! O Ekajaṭī, great rākṣasī, you with three eyes, whose form is fierce and terrifying, who causes fear to all beings, you who are fierce and possess fierce prowess, thunderbolt of blood, you of great speed, pacifier of all beings: rend, rend! tear asunder, tear asunder! destroy, destroy! bring forth, bring forth! Accept this offering of perfume, flowers, incense, and bali—svāhā!

Oṃ! Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to the noble Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Great Compassionate One! Oṃ! O Ekajaṭī, three-eyed one, you who wear an elephant hide as an upper garment, adorned with serpents, whose body is fashioned from skulls, you who dwell always on the shore of the ocean; you reside in the midst of Laṅkā, having honored Rāmaṇa. Who, who, in the midst of trembling? You are the destroyer of obstacles for the practitioner! Caḥ caḥ, you who shake your head! La la la! You who hold a lump of flesh in your hand, you devour a thousand men of flesh! Hāhākāre! O you of the red banner! You whose body is fashioned from jewels, gold, and lapis lazuli! You whose voice resounds with the cries of crows, cranes, blue jays, and partridges! In the fierce mass of flames like sparks from wood, resounding with the cries of severed heroes (*ruṇḍavīra*)—hurry, hurry! Come, come! Fill it yourself! Do not delay! Ehy ehi! Ho ho ho! Hrī hrī hrī! He he he! Tiṭi tiṭi! Miṭi miṭi! Strike down my enemies, all obstacles, all malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*), and all misfortune! Attract the glory of Śrī! O Ekajaṭī, svāhā! Three-eyed one, svāhā! One who has gone to the three refuges, svāhā!

This *ekajaṭī* is a subsidiary heart-mantra (*upahṛdaya*) that performs all rites; it accomplishes the rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and malevolent sorcery (*abhicāraka*). One should always perform the yoga-meditation on the heart of this *ekajaṭī*. And what is that supreme heart-mantra? Oṃ bhagavati ekajaṭi hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā.

This is the supreme heart-mantra of the Bhagavatī: Ehy ehi Ekajaṭi! Roar, roar! Dispel, dispel all obstacles! Crush, crush! Destroy, destroy! Devour, devour! Drive mad, drive mad! Kill, kill! Slay, slay! O Bhagavatī, accomplisher of all aims, svāhā!

By this binding of the directions, by the upper binding, and by the binding of the topknot, there is the binding (and protection) against all [beings], such as lions, tigers, yakṣas, ḍākinīs, serpents, mice, and so forth, upon entering the cremation ground.
These are the invocation mantras for the four world-protectors and others who are stationed all around the womb-maṇḍala.

Oṃ, svāhā to Indra, lord of gods and asuras! Oṃ, svāhā to Agni! Oṃ, homage to Yama, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Vaivasvata, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the lord of the terrifying rākṣasas, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Varuṇa, lord of the nāgas, svāhā! Oṃ, svāhā to Vāyu in the northwest! Oṃ, homage to Kubera, lord of wealth, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Īśāna, lord of spirits, svāhā!

These are the mantras for invoking the deities of the directions. Then, having performed a magnificent worship according to the procedure taught in the Tantra, and having offered magnificent sacrificial oblations, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciple. Having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth, one should cause all the rites to be carried out.
Now follows the procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna) of the Blessed One Ekajaṭī.

Having purchased a rag from a cemetery by means of a "hero's purchase" (*vīrakraya*), and having become a consumer of meat, one should have the Blessed Lady painted by a pure painter who wears clean garments and possesses all the required characteristics. She has three faces, the color of a blue lotus, a flat nose, upward-pointing hair, large eyes, and three eyes; her lips hang down, her face is terrifying with protruding fangs, and she has four arms. She wears a garland fashioned from skulls, is adorned with ornaments of snakes, and is decorated with the tips of severed hands. Her mouth is situated in the middle of a skull, her tongue is curled back, and blood flows from her throat; she rests upon a skull, has a protruding belly, is clothed in a tiger skin, and wears an elephant hide as an upper garment. In her hands she holds a noose, a goad, and a spear; she should be painted according to these specific characteristics.
Having purchased by means of a "hero's price" (*vīrakrayeṇa*), [the Blessed Lady] (*bhagavatī*)— clad in garments (*vastra*).
It should be painted; [the reading is] *citrāpayitavyā* (emended), [against] *citrāpayitravyā* (manuscript).
[The reading is] *kapālamadhyamukhā* (conjectured), [against] *kapolamadhyemukhe* (manuscript).

To the side of the Goddess, one should depict Dīrghabāhu in a dwarf form, with his own limbs [emaciated], wearing an elephant hide as an upper garment and a tiger skin as a lower garment. Seated upon a deer-throne, he should be drawn holding a vessel for sprinkling the enemy with both hands. Above him, a son of the gods stands upon a cloud, beating a drum; there are also clouds accompanied by lightning. Below him, one should depict the purifier (the officiant), his hand occupied with an incense burner.

[They] sounded the drum. Then, having placed the painted cloth behind him exactly as it was drawn, and having performed worship according to his means, having offered various kinds of food and drink along with a generous sacrificial oblation (*bali*), an offering of food (*naivedya*), and garlands, having bathed at the three times of day, changing his clothes three times, abstaining from liquor and meat, and wearing clean garments, he should face the east and recite the supreme heart-mantra consisting of three syllables until one hundred thousand [times].

Facing east, a great sound arises and an earthquake occurs; there is a trembling of the cloth and a trembling of the garland—these are the rootless omens. One must not be afraid; an *argha* offering should be presented with sandalwood water and fragrant flowers, using this mantra.

O Blessed One, Ekajaṭī, wearer of the illusion of a rākṣasī, you who have taken up the training precepts of the three refuges, speaker of truth: *dhuru* 3, *dhara* 3, O giver of boons! Accept this water-offering (*argha*). O Blessed One, homage, homage, *svāhā*!

Then, her face smiling and possessing a divine form, she says: "O Vidyādhara, I am pleased; choose seven boons. These are: sovereignty, the state of a Vidyādhara, mastery over the gods, the power of moving through the sky, the attainment of a Yakṣiṇī, and the attainment of the elixir of immortality (rasāyana).
"I am pleased. Then, the ritual actions of the Blessed One Ekajaṭī are as follows:
one who desires to perform a rite of pacification (*śāntika*) should offer eight thousand oblations of *apāmārga* wood fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

One who desires to perform a rite for the peace of a house should smear and plaster the entire mandala of the house, offer a bali-oblation to the spirits, kindle a fire with *devadāru* wood, and offer eight thousand oblations of black sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; thus all calamities will be pacified. One who desires to perform a rite for the peace of cattle should offer eight thousand oblations of cow-dung smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; thus there will be peace for the cattle. One who desires to perform a rite for the peace of a person should offer eight thousand oblations of barley, wheat, and *nāgakesara* flowers; thus there will be peace for the person.

One desiring to perform a rite for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*) should subsist on a diet of milk and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), kindle a fire with *jaṭā* wood, and offer eight thousand oblations of fine rice (*paramānna*). Within seven days, one beholds a great treasure.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of barley grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee for seven days; one obtains ten *pala* of gold. Having combined *nāgakeśara*, lotus filaments, red flowers, and turmeric into one, and having mixed them with *śāli* rice, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of these [grains] smeared with ghee and honey; one obtains one hundred thousand *suvarṇa*. One should mix the marrow of *hariṣṭaka* seeds with pungent oil and perform this daily at the time of the sun’s setting (*akākorttare*); one obtains twenty *pala* of gold.

One should offer oblations mixed with beef, guggulu, and clarified butter for seven days; one then obtains five excellent villages. If the rite is not yet accomplished, one obtains a village consisting of a thousand households (*sahasrapiṇḍa*).

Having combined buffalo blood and goat blood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *raktapāṭala* flowers smeared with pungent oil for ten days; [the deity] then bestows ten thousand vessels made of copper.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of *mālatī* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains a thousand *dīnāras*. Having combined *śatāvarī*, *vibhītaka*, and marrow together, one should offer eight thousand oblations smeared with curd and honey; one obtains a well-adorned and very beautiful maiden. One should offer the flour of *śāli* rice mixed with pungent oil for seven days; one obtains a silver *lakṣa*.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of barley grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. No one becomes poor after this has been offered.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of mustard seeds; it constantly provides for one's expenses.
One should offer eight thousand *atimuktaka* flowers; he gives a hundred garments quickly. One should offer eight thousand *kunda* buds; one obtains ten million pairs of garments.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of red flowers and red sandalwood; one becomes the lord of a region.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds, honey, and ghee smeared with cow urine; or twenty-one [oblations], and one becomes a recipient of all ornaments and obtains them.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of white sesame, *gaula* grass, mustard, and *kaṇḍula* stalks smeared with curd, ghee, and honey for seven days; [then] one possesses the very strength of an elephant.
*Note:* *Kaṇḍula* is a type of reed.

Having kindled a fire with *suvarṇapṛthikā* wood from Gauḍa or Guḍa, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *suvarṇapṛthikā* flowers smeared with pungent oil. This bestows the sovereignty of a neighboring kingdom.

By means of the root mantra of the Blessed One Ekajaṭī, one should touch the right foot of the noble Avalokiteśvara with a thousand *atasī* flowers for twenty-one days; this brings about the sovereignty of a neighboring kingdom.
One should offer a thousand *pāṭala* flowers; one will receive the binding of a turban (*paṭṭabandha*).
One should offer eight thousand parched grains (*lāja*) smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; there will be an increase in grain.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of parched grain (*lāja*) soaked in oil; there will be an increase in all requisites. Having kindled the fire with fuel-sticks of *udumbara*, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *śālmalī* flowers; it becomes a protective circle for the house.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of flowers shaped like the *karṇikā*. Incense made of "great flesh" (*mahāmāṃsa*) should be offered; a stream of wealth (*vasudhārā*) will fall. Having mixed goat fat and buffalo blood together, one should offer them over the embers of *khadira* wood; one beholds a great treasure.
Having mixed one's own blood, goat blood, and crow blood together, one should offer them; whatever one desires, that very thing is accomplished.
% NB: Human flesh, one’s own blood, and so forth.
The Chapter on Nourishing Rites (Pauṣṭikapaṭala).
[The Chapter on Prosperity] Oṃ!

Blessed One, Ekajaṭī, dweller on the shore of the ocean, fierce one, of fierce prowess, worshipped by the conqueror of the three worlds, you whose strength and valor are unimpeded: come here, come here! Enter this human body; descend, descend! Paralyze, paralyze! Delude, delude! Roar, roar! Crush, crush! Shatter, shatter! Enter and fill it! Speak of the past, future, and present exactly as they are! Svāhā! This is the mantra for the descent of the deity into one's own self.

Alternatively, one who desires to bring a king under control should take clay from the gate of the king’s palace, kindle a fire with *rājārka* wood, and offer a mixture of mustard seeds and salt as an oblation. The king will become submissive.
Regarding salt:

one who desires to bring a royal minister under control should combine parched grain (*lāja*), *yava*, and *agakesara*, and offer them into the fire eight thousand times; he will be brought under control. One who desires to bring a royal minister under control should offer parched grain eight thousand times; he will be brought under control.

Desiring to bring the king’s wife under his control, one should kindle a fire with pomegranate wood, fashion an image of butter, cut it with a sharp weapon, and offer it into the fire eight thousand times. She will become submissive.

Desiring to bring a Kṣatriya under one's control, one should offer as an oblation the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) of the Blessed One Ekajaṭī together with oil-cake (*piṇyāka*). He becomes submissive. Desiring to bring a Caṇḍālī woman under one's control, one should offer as an oblation husks, cow-hair, and pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*). She becomes submissive.
And one who desires to bring a brahmin under control should offer oblations of barley flour smeared with pungent oil; he becomes submissive.

One who desires to bring a Śūdra woman under his control should combine *rajaḥpuṣpa*, peacock feathers, and red *śāli* rice; having anointed these with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), he should offer eight thousand oblations. She becomes submissive.

One who desires to bring a Vaiśya woman under his control should offer eight thousand oblations of wheat, mustard seeds, salt, and pungent oil, having anointed them [with pungent oil]. She enters into servitude.

Desiring to bring a bhikṣuṇī under one's control: having made a mandala with a limb [of a corpse] and having prepared a wick made from a bhikṣu’s robe, one should stir it with goat fat and offer it as an oblation; she becomes submissive. Desiring to bring a bhikṣu of great supernatural power (maharddhika) under one's control: having gathered together black gram (māṣa), beans (muṣa), and vacā, one should offer eight thousand oblations of them smeared with buffalo ghee; he becomes submissive. Desiring to bring a courtesan (veśyā) under one's control: one should offer eight thousand oblations of cow-dung smeared with black salt (kṛṣṇalavana); she becomes submissive.

One who desires to bring a Śūdra woman under one's control should offer eight thousand oblations of powdered ginger, salt, and parched grain (lāja). She becomes submissive. One who desires to bring a maiden under one's control should offer oblations of *dvīpiśatru* (the enemy of the leopard, i.e., the tiger); she becomes submissive.

One who desires to bring a city under control should go to a river flowing through the city, cast oil-cake flowers and brick powder into the river, and recite the vidyā one hundred and eight times. All [the inhabitants] will become submissive; all the chief ministers and people will bow down like ears of grain. One who desires to bring an elephant under control should offer eight thousand *āmra* flowers as oblations. A rutting elephant becomes submissive.

One who desires to bring an elephant under control should kindle a fire with *nāga* wood, make it red with *nāgakesara*, yellow orpiment, and vermilion, and offer oblations near a lake inhabited by *nāgas*. A *nāga* maiden, adorned with all ornaments, will emerge, seize [the elephant], and lead it inside; it becomes submissive.
Thus ends the chapter on subduing through the Blessed One Ekajaṭī.

Now follow the rites of sorcery (*abhicārakarman*) belonging to the Blessed Lady Ekajaṭī. Having put on blue garments and a yellow sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and making wrath itself the standard, one should take the dust from the feet of the enemy, fashion an image (*pratikṛti*) of him, cover it with a piece of deep red silk cloth, and cast it into a serpent pool (*nāgahrada*). It is seized by the Gandhināga, and all manner of diseases afflict the enemy.
Having covered [the fire] with a deep red silk cloth,
one who desires to destroy enemies should kindle a funeral pyre and offer eight thousand oblations of horse gram (*kulattha*) soaked in pungent oil. Immediately, the enemies will be destroyed.
Having kindled a fire with *kovidāra* wood, one should offer oblations of *rājikā* seeds soaked in poison and blood; this results in [the subjugation] of a *yakṣa*.

Having made an image out of cow-dung that has not fallen [to the ground], and having mixed it with red mustard seeds, one should bury it on a riverbank; [the victim] is seized by the disease of boils (*sphoṭiroga*).

Having climbed a dry tree, while wearing a wet garment or a wet cloth and eating wet food, one should recite the mantra facing the sun while grasping the name [of the target]; as soon as the wet cloth dries, [the target] dies right there.
Having kindled a fire with *kaṇṭhaka* wood fuel, one should offer *kaṇṭhaka* wood eight thousand times. [The victim] will be seized by Śeṣanāga.

One should grind [the victim] together with a snake-skin; reciting the mantra while grasping the name [of the victim], one should cause them to be struck by the embers of *khadira* wood. The enemy will be seized by the disease of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).

Having read this on April 24, 2014: On the twenty-fourth day of the month of Āśvina, one should mix the fruit of the *śālmalī* tree with honey; then, having placed together the blood of a snake, the blood of a corpse, and flowers used as ritual offerings (*nirmālya*), one should offer them into the fire after anointing them with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*). Alternatively, for the purpose of causing a flow of blood, one should place together the horn of a rhinoceros, the fruit of the *vaṃtara*, and poison mixed with *karahāla*, anoint them with salt, and offer them into the fire while uttering the name of the enemy. At night, one should offer horse dung, lac, and the fruit of the *kaṭuturu* tree, anointed with pungent oil, while uttering the name of the enemy; [the enemy] will become insane.
Having combined crow’s blood, lizard’s blood, and pigeon’s dung into one, one should offer them as an oblation; [the victim] will suffer from bloody diarrhea.

Having combined horse’s blood and horse’s urine into one, one should saturate red mustard seeds with it and recite the vidyā one hundred and eight times. With that incense, [the eyes] become possessed by the deity;
by offering an oblation of cow-dung, the enemy becomes free from passion.
The chapter on malevolent rites (abhicāra) is completed.
We shall now explain the chapter on the disappearance of the Blessed Lady.

Oṃ! Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to the noble Avalokiteśvara! Homage to Ekajaṭā, the great rākṣasī, whose tongue is like lightning, whose fangs are lolling, O Blessed One who moves through the sky, whose prowess is unimpeded, whose movement is everywhere unobstructed! Protect my body, protect my body with the powers of aṇimā, garimā, mahimā, and laghimā; conceal my body, conceal it in a shadow-like state; deprive others of their power; make yourself invisible, svāhā! Svāhā to the Buddha! Svāhā to the Dharma! Svāhā to the Saṅgha! Svāhā to the Pratyekabuddha! Homage to the noble Avalokiteśvara! To Ekajaṭā: bring them here, bring them here! O Great Fierce One! Seize them, seize them! Guard them, guard them! Conquer them, conquer them! O Viguṇi, svāhā! Svāhā to Māyāvatī! Svāhā to Raudrī! Svāhā to Mohā! Homage to Ākāśagāminī, svāhā! Homage to those who move on the earth, svāhā! Homage to those who move in the sky, svāhā! Homage to those who move in the water, svāhā! Homage to those who move in the clouds, svāhā! Homage to those who move in the path of the wind, svāhā! Roar, roar! Fight, fight! Battle, battle! Crush, crush! Manifest transformations, manifest transformations! O Uneven One! Cause to disperse, cause to disperse! Whether it be in the clouds or throughout the entire world, let it be so! O Ekajaṭī, great rākṣasī, come! Disappear within, disappear! Homage, svāhā!

This is the science of invisibility (*antardhāna-vidyā*). It must not be given to a son; it must not be given to an unworthy disciple. This is the supreme accomplishment. The science of invisibility of Ekajaṭā must not be disclosed. One should fill the skull of a black cat with earth from a mountain cave and cause it to be placed upon the breast. Having combined two sprouts, goat’s blood, *gocana*, *brahmahaṇḍī*, and *nāgakesara* into one, and having offered a blood-oblation (*rudhirabali*) to the Blessed One Ekajaṭā, one should empower it with eight thousand recitations and then begin the practice for twenty-one days; thus one becomes invisible.

Alternatively, one should place collyrium in the heart of the corpse of one who has died naturally and leave it for seven nights. One should burn it in seven fires of *citrā*. With eyes anointed by that, one becomes invisible for seven days.

Having taken a wild mouse, one should place a thousand applications of collyrium and yellow orpiment into its eyes. One should burn it with fire from the house of a *caṇḍāla*. Having performed a grand worship of the Blessed Lady Ekajaṭī, one should empower it eight thousand times before her and recite the mantra over the eyes. One becomes invisible for five nights.

Having taken the hair from the ear of a tawny cow, having placed five of them together in front of that very cow, having wrapped them in fifteen pieces of refined gold, and having cast them into a cluster of *bhallātaka* fruits; having performed worship to the Blessed Noble Tārā and given food to the *ekajaṭī* monks; and having made seven mandala-offerings before the Blessed Buddha with red sandalwood and placed [the substance] in the hollow of one's joined palms, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times in its presence. One becomes a traveler through the sky.

Having gone to a cemetery that is surrounded by unbroken [grain], one should smear a mandala with cow dung. Having placed a corpse right there and performed a grand worship, one should offer oblations of *bali*, food offerings, and fuel-sticks into the fire; one should then sacrifice white mustard seeds smeared with the blood of a *kāśa* (?). The corpse rises up. Then, having offered perfumes, incense, *bali*, and food offerings, and having adorned it with various ornaments—decorating it with bracelets, armlets, bangles, and rings—one should strike it with a *catmākṣa* (?). Then, with this mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions, the binding of the mandala, the binding below, and the binding above: "O Ekajaṭī, holder of the Great Illusion, O you of great speed, O wanderer in the sky! Jiṭi 2, vidya 2, le 2, hī 2, ṭi 2! Move by means of the mantra of the Vidyādharas! At midnight, one should sacrifice eight thousand pills of *guggulu* smeared with clarified butter with the root mantra. Then the sword blazes; it makes [the world] pure with the sounds *ciṭi piṭi*. Then one becomes accomplished (*siddha*). Then, taking the yellow sword, one travels through the sky and becomes a king of the Vidyādharas.

Having powdered goat meat, one should fashion an image of a she-goat with that flesh. One should cover it with a peacock feather. Having performed worship of the Bhagavatī, one should place it before her and recite the mantra ten thousand times. A *śālali* (porcupine quill) should be offered in front of her; she will eat it. Then success (*siddhi*) occurs. One should cut open the belly of that she-goat with a weapon. One should eat the kidling from its womb together with ghee and honey. [The mantra is: "O you who have the color of the rising sun, you who have entered the womb, svāhā! Having placed the face of that corpse in the midst of the body and sitting upon it, one should offer a thousand oblations of *paramānna* (milk-rice). That corpse rises up. One becomes a vehicle equal to Garuḍa. One has a retinue of twenty *vidyādharas*. One obtains eight *vidyādharī* maidens. One wanders together with them. One remains for an eon (*kalpa*).

One who desires to accomplish the *khaḍgavidyādhara* [attainment] should have a sword made of flower-metal under the Puṣya asterism. Beginning with all fragrances the size of a thumb, one should place it before a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics or before an image. Having performed extensive offerings and worship, one should recite the mantra day by day, grasping it with both hands, for one month. At the end of three nights, one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair; with hair curled in ringlets, one becomes a sky-walker and lives for thousands of years.

Taking a peacock’s eye-feather (*mayūracandrikā*) measuring two cubits and numbering two hundred and twenty, one should purify it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), wash it with water from the seven sacred fords (*saptatīrtha*), and, having fashioned a mandala before a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics or before an image, perform a grand worship. Having offered *guggulu* incense, one should recite the mantra for twenty-one days. Then, one should have a circle made of ivory measuring two spans (*dvivitasti*). One should have it made while reciting the root mantra of the Blessed One Ekajaṭī. Having smeared a mandala with red sandalwood, red flowers should be offered. Having performed a grand worship, one should offer a sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtabali*) and food offerings, and recite the root-vidyā eight thousand times. Then the peacock-feather wand (*picchaka*) releases the excellent peacock and flies up to the height of two cubits. Thereupon, it becomes perfected (*siddha*). By merely whirling that wand, it brings forth food and other provisions, snakes, bedding, requisites, garments, perfumes, flowers, sandalwood, agallochum, divine garments, and various ornaments, providing them to the body. At all times, one experiences the bliss of the earth, the heavens, and the Vidyādharas.

During the dark fortnight, in a temple of Śiva, or in a cremation ground, on a mountain, or in a grove, one should stand facing south at night and perform a grand worship, offering a *bali* and food oblation for all spirits. Having fashioned a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from the hair of a woman and placed it before [the deity], one should recite the mantra eight thousand times. One should grind the flesh of a man who is either holding a sword in his hand or is suspended [by it] together with *guggulu* resin. Having made pellets the size of a jujube seed (*badara*), one should recite the mantra eight thousand times. Then, the cloth will tremble, or there will be a great roar, or it will fill the space with flashes of flame. One must not be afraid; then all success (*siddhi*) is attained. The Blessed One herself becomes present in the vicinity of Noble Avalokiteśvara. Afterwards, one attains the Noble Truths through the essence of the mantra: *Oṃ vedmi ri 2 tasni ri 2 krama krāmati vikrame vahi 2 mavikuru 2 bhara 2 siddhe susiddhe oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā.* This mantra is perfected. It is the unimpeded heart-mantra of Ekajaṭī, which brings success through mere recitation.

One should have an umbrella made from birch bark or *kaṭuka* wood; [an image of] a peacock should be made from *siddhi* wood. One should have a pair of wooden sandals (*pādukā*) made. Having placed those two—the umbrella and the sandals—in a shrine (*caitya*) or a house containing relics (*sadhātuka*), one should perform a grand worship and offer one hundred and eight oblations every day for seven days. On the eighth day, at the time of midnight, having gone to a solitary tree, one should take the umbrella, step upon the wooden sandals, apply twenty drops of one’s own blood, offer a great sacrifice to the elements (*mahābhūtabali*), and recite the mantra. One becomes a traveler through the sky. With this mantra: *Oṃ ciri 2 vicara 2 Ekajaṭī commands: lu hūṃ svāhā*. Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to the noble Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion! Homage to Ekajaṭā, the great Rākṣasī, who has taken refuge in the Triple Gem and the training precepts (*śikṣāpada*). I am released from the womb of a Rākṣasī, O you who set in motion the truth of the Dharma! O Ekajaṭī, O Trirakṣī, O terrifier of all beings, O wielder of Indra’s thunderbolt! Terrify 2! Crush 2! Manifest transformations 2! Shatter 2! Grind to powder! Smash! Tātava 2! O Victorious One, svāhā! Tārā commands: svāhā!

This is the heart-entrancing ritual procedure for this vidyā. Having become one who subsists on alms from monks, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite the heart-mantra one thousand times. Even if one has been breast-fed by a mother, she appears before one; one beholds all the goddesses; one beholds the fissures of the netherworld (pātāla); and all one's undertakings are accomplished. In all rites of accomplishment, an offering (argha) must be presented. One should constantly keep it in mind, and one becomes a son [of the deity]. In brief, it performs all activities.

During a lunar eclipse, having smeared a mandala and having placed together one *prastha* each of *pippala*, white mustard seeds, and *bhṛṅgarāja* in a metal vessel, one should recite the mantra until only water remains. Having removed that [liquid], one should mix the powder of *karañja* and the powder of lotus filaments together and pour them into that very [vessel]. Having performed worship of the Blessed Noble Avalokiteśvara, one should continue reciting until one no longer hears the screeching of mice; then one becomes accomplished (*siddha*). By anointing one's feet with that same medicinal herb, one can travel a hundred *yojanas* and return. This is the mantra for walking upon this [earth]: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ, homage to Ekajaṭī! Spread forth, spread forth! Move, move! Lame, lame! O you who possess a body of wind and dust! Maṭa hūṃ svāhā!
The third chapter, the mantra for walking on foot, is thus completed.
Now we shall explain the chapter on Pātāla belonging to the Blessed One Ekajaṭī.
Neither a lunar day (tithi), nor a constellation (nakṣatra), nor a fast (upavāsa) is prescribed.

Having gone to the entrance of the cave of the Asuras, one should place goat’s blood, black mustard seeds, salt, and the best of horns together in one spot, and offer eight thousand oblations of them soaked in pungent oil. This causes the hearts of the Asura maidens to tremble, and they lead [the practitioner] inside. He sports with them until, in the sixth month, he enters the path of Viṣṇu. At that time, the syllable *hūṃ* must be released; then he enters once more with his discus. His mantra is as follows:
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Ekajaṭī! O you who laugh, O restrainer! Oṃ ṭhari 2, ṭaṭṭā! Scatter 2, crush 2, shatter 2, suck 2, cause all mantras to fall, phaṭ svāhā!

The ritual procedure for this mantra is as follows: one should recite it ten thousand times while subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*). Thereupon, it becomes perfected. Through its perfection, the accomplishment of the netherworld (*pātāla*) is attained.

Oṃ, homage! Come, O Blessed One, Ekajaṭī! Fill yourself and others! Raṇa 2! For the sake of the fulfillment of glory and desire, svāhā! To Śriyā, svāhā! To Mahāśriyā, svāhā! To Bālā, svāhā! To Atibalā, svāhā! To the one who crushes all gods and asuras, svāhā! Oṃ, homage! O Blessed One, Ekajaṭī, three-eyed one, you who strike with the triple-pointed weapon, you who hold a peacock-feather fan in your hand, you whose weapon is leaves! Tear, tear! Rend, rend! Cut, cut! Split, split! Strike, strike! Kill the enemies, kill them! Hūṃ 3! Phaṭ 3! Duru 2! [Strike] the heart! Svāhā!
By means of this vidyā, one slays enemies; one paralyzes water and paralyzes fire. These are the supreme heart-mantras of the Blessed One Ekajaṭī: Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hrāṃ is the supreme heart-mantra.

Oṃ jaṭa 2 vāmajaṭe hūṃ phaṭ, [this is] for the head (śiraḥ). Oṃ trijaṭe hūṃ phaṭ, [this is] for the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ jaṭāmakuṭadhāraṇi bhagavati hana 2 hūṃ phaṭ, [this is] for the weapon (astram).

Oṃ bhagavati hūṃ jaṭi 2 svāhā. [This is] the armor (*kavaca*). Oṃ, homage! O Blessed One, Ekajaṭī, Great Rākṣasī, come! Accept this offering of perfume, flowers, incense, and bali, O Blessed One! Svāhā! Oṃ Ekajaṭī, rararara, you who move with ferocity, stay, stay! Remember your pledge! Accomplish all my tasks, accomplish them! Svāhā!

Oṃ trāsani 2 trāsaya 2 bhṛkuṭi jaṭi vaijaṭi ṭha ṭha treṃ bhṛkuṭī phaṭ ṭha ṭha. It causes [the enemy] to seize, causes suffering, causes to rise up, and causes to be expelled; it accomplishes all purposes and all servile rites (ceṭikarmāṇi).

At the conclusion of the meal, a morsel of food should be offered. *Oṃ namo ratnatrayāya nama ekajaṭyā mahārākṣasyāś ceṭīnāṃ hṛdayamantraḥ*: *Oṃ cali rakṣatha māṃ ucchiṣṭasyānucchiṣṭaṃ vā śītalatvapratipannasya vā hara 2 mara 2 hara 2 bhrāmaya śatrūn troṭaya sphoṭaya mūrdhānaṃ hara jīvitaṃ śatrūṇāṃ mahārākṣasi ekajaṭī samājñāpayati svāhā*.
And this maidservant must always be given the remains of the food.
The ritual manual of the Blessed Noble Ekajaṭī is completed.

May there be prosperity! In the year 749, on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, under the constellation Uttaraphālgunī, in the Siddhi yoga, on Thursday. On this very day, the *Ekajaṭikalpa* is completed along with its ritual manual (*sādhana*). By whatever merit [accrues from] this, it was written for his own spiritual benefit by the Vajrācārya Śrī Candradeva, residing at the Guṇadeva Vihāra. May there be auspiciousness for all the world; may you be the object of their heart’s desires. May there be auspiciousness for all the world; may you be the object of their heart’s desires. || || ||
